topics.title: The Request Object (req)
topics.summary: req carries params, query, body, headers, cookies, IP and URL details for the incoming request.
topics.description:
The `req` object describes everything the client sent. Knowing its properties by heart makes handlers easy to write.

### Where does the data come from?
| Property | Source | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `req.params` | path `/users/:id` | strings |
| `req.query` | after `?` | strings/arrays; read-only getter in v5 |
| `req.body` | request payload | needs `express.json()` / `urlencoded()`; `undefined` otherwise |
| `req.headers` / `req.get('name')` | HTTP headers | header names are lower-case in `req.headers` |
| `req.cookies` | `Cookie` header | needs `cookie-parser` |
| `req.signedCookies` | signed cookies | needs `cookie-parser(secret)` |

### URL-related properties
- `req.method` - `GET`, `POST`...
- `req.originalUrl` - full URL with query (`/api/v1/users?x=1`), never changes.
- `req.baseUrl` - the router mount path (`/api/v1`).
- `req.path` - path without query string, relative to the mount point.
- `req.protocol`, `req.secure`, `req.hostname`. In Express 5 `req.host` includes the port while `req.hostname` does not.

### Client details
`req.ip` is the client address. Behind a proxy (nginx, Heroku, Render, Cloudflare) it shows the proxy IP unless you tell Express to trust it: `app.set('trust proxy', 1)`. Then `req.ip` uses `X-Forwarded-For` and `req.protocol` uses `X-Forwarded-Proto`.

### Helpers
- `req.get('Content-Type')` reads a header case-insensitively.
- `req.is('json')` checks the request content type.
- `req.accepts('json')` inspects the `Accept` header.
- `req.xhr`, `req.fresh`/`req.stale` for caching logic.

### Custom data
Attach your own fields (`req.user`, `req.requestId`). They live only for that request.
keyPoints: `params` = path, `query` = after `?`, `body` = payload, `headers`, `cookies`
`originalUrl` vs `baseUrl` vs `path` differ inside mounted routers
Set `trust proxy` behind a reverse proxy to get the real `req.ip`
Use `req.get()` or `req.headers['lower-case']` for headers
Add custom fields like `req.user` in middleware
pitfalls: Trusting `X-Forwarded-For` blindly by setting `trust proxy` to `true` without a proxy in front

examples.title: Inspecting a request
examples.code:
import express from 'express'
import cookieParser from 'cookie-parser'

const app = express()
app.set('trust proxy', 1)          // we sit behind one proxy
app.use(express.json())
app.use(cookieParser())

app.post('/api/v1/debug/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    method: req.method,
    params: req.params,
    query: req.query,
    body: req.body,
    auth: req.get('authorization') ?? null,
    cookies: req.cookies,
    ip: req.ip,
    originalUrl: req.originalUrl,
    path: req.path,
    isJson: Boolean(req.is('json')),
  })
})

app.listen(3000)

interview.q: Difference between req.originalUrl, req.baseUrl and req.path?
interview.a: originalUrl is the full requested URL; baseUrl is the router's mount prefix; path is the remainder after the mount point without the query string.

interview.q: How do you get the real client IP behind nginx?
interview.a: Set app.set('trust proxy', 1) (or the exact number of proxies) so Express reads X-Forwarded-For for req.ip.

topics.title: The Response Object (res)
topics.summary: Use res.status, json, send, sendStatus, set, end and locals to craft responses correctly.
topics.description:
`res` is how you answer. Most of your code ends with one of these methods.

### Sending bodies
- `res.send(data)` - sends a string, Buffer, object or array. Content-Type is chosen automatically (HTML for strings, JSON for objects).
- `res.json(obj)` - always JSON (`Content-Type: application/json`). Prefer it in APIs because it also converts `null`/`undefined` safely.
- `res.end()` - ends with no body (low-level).
- `res.sendStatus(404)` - sets the status and sends its text (`Not Found`) as the body.

### Status
`res.status(201)` sets the status code and returns `res`, so you can chain: `res.status(201).json(user)`. In Express 5 the code must be an integer between 100 and 999; passing a string throws. The v4 forms `res.json(status, obj)` and `res.send(status, body)` were removed.

### Headers
`res.set('X-Total-Count', '42')` (alias `res.header`), `res.type('json')`, `res.location('/users/5')`, `res.append('Set-Cookie', ...)`, `res.vary('Accept')`.

### `res.locals`
An object whose properties live for the request. Middleware can store data (`res.locals.user`) for later handlers and templates.

### 204 and empty bodies
For deletes, respond with `res.status(204).end()` - a 204 must not have a body.

### One response only
After `res.json()` the headers are sent. A second `res.send()` throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. Use `return res.json(...)` in guard clauses.

### Rendering views
`res.render('page', data)` uses a template engine (EJS, Pug, Handlebars). In JSON APIs you rarely need it.
keyPoints: `res.status(code).json(data)` is the standard API reply
`res.send` guesses the type, `res.json` is always JSON
`res.sendStatus(n)` sends the code and its default text
204 means no content: use `.end()`
Use `return` with early responses to avoid double sends
pitfalls: `res.json` twice in one request (headers already sent)
Express 4 habits that fail in 5: `res.json(200, obj)`, `res.sendfile`, `res.send(404)`

examples.title: Common responses

interview.a: Both send a body; res.send picks the Content-Type from the data, while res.json always serialises to JSON with the JSON content type.

interview.q: Why do you see "Cannot set headers after they are sent"?
interview.a: Because the handler tried to send a second response (or write headers) after the first was already sent, usually from a missing return.

topics.title: Redirect, sendFile and Download
topics.summary: Redirect clients, send files and force downloads safely with absolute paths and a root option.
topics.description:
### Redirects
`res.redirect('/login')` sends **302 Found** by default. Pass a status as the first argument for permanent moves: `res.redirect(301, '/new-url')`. Use **303** after a POST so the browser follows with GET, and **307/308** to keep the method. In Express 5 the magic string `'back'` no longer works (it would redirect to a literal URL called "back"); use `req.get('Referer') || '/'`.

### `res.sendFile()`
Streams a file with correct MIME type, ETag and range support. The path must be **absolute**, or you must pass a `root`:

```js
res.sendFile('report.pdf', { root: path.join(import.meta.dirname, 'files') })
```

Using `root` also protects against path traversal such as `../../etc/passwd`. Never pass raw user input as the path without `root`. The v4 spelling `res.sendfile` is gone.

### `res.download()`
Same as `sendFile` but sets `Content-Disposition: attachment` so the browser saves the file. Optional second argument is the filename the user sees:

```js
res.download('/abs/path/invoice-17.pdf', 'Invoice.pdf')
```

### Errors
Both accept a callback: `res.sendFile(file, opts, (err) => { if (err) next(err) })`. A missing file produces a 404 error object with `err.status`.

### When to use what
| Need | Method |
|---|---|
| Show an HTML page / image inline | `sendFile` |
| Force "Save as..." | `download` |
| Send generated data as a file | set headers + `res.send(buffer)` or stream |
| Server-rendered page | `render` |

### Single Page Apps
Serve `index.html` for unknown routes with `res.sendFile(path.join(dist, 'index.html'))` as the last `GET` handler.
keyPoints: `res.redirect(url)` is 302; pass 301/303/307/308 for other behaviours
`res.sendFile` needs an absolute path or `{ root }`
`res.download(path, name)` forces a download
Use `root` to stop path traversal
v5 removed `res.sendfile` and `redirect('back')`
pitfalls: Passing user-controlled filenames without `root` or validation
Redirecting to a user-supplied URL (open redirect vulnerability)

examples.title: Redirect, sendFile and download
What the client sees
examples.code:
curl -i localhost:3000/old-page
# HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
# Location: /new-page

curl -i localhost:3000/download/report
# Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=Monthly-Report.pdf
# Content-Type: application/pdf

interview.a: sendFile shows the file inline (browser may render it); download sets Content-Disposition: attachment to make the browser save it.

interview.q: How do you prevent path traversal when serving user-requested files?
interview.a: Use the root option (or resolve and verify the final path stays inside the allowed directory) and never concatenate raw input into a path.

topics.title: Headers, Cookies and Content Negotiation
topics.summary: Read and set headers, handle cookies with cookie-parser and respond in the format the client asks for.
topics.description:
### Headers
Read with `req.get('Authorization')`; write with `res.set('X-Request-Id', id)`. Common ones: `Content-Type`, `Authorization`, `Accept`, `Cache-Control`, `Location`, `Set-Cookie`. Custom headers traditionally start with `X-`. Express adds `X-Powered-By: Express`, which you should disable (`app.disable('x-powered-by')` or use helmet) to avoid advertising your stack.

### Cookies
A cookie is a small key-value pair stored by the browser and sent back automatically.
- `res.cookie('name', 'value', options)` sets one.
- `res.clearCookie('name')` removes it (use the same `path`/`domain`).
- Reading requires the **cookie-parser** middleware: `app.use(cookieParser())`, then `req.cookies.name`.
- Options: `httpOnly` (JavaScript cannot read it), `secure` (HTTPS only), `sameSite` (`'lax' | 'strict' | 'none'`), `maxAge` (milliseconds), `signed: true` (tamper-proof with a secret).

### Content negotiation
Clients say what they accept in the `Accept` header. `req.accepts(['json','html'])` returns the best match, and `res.format({...})` runs the handler for the best match, answering **406 Not Acceptable** (or your `default`) when none fit. `Accept-Language`, `Accept-Encoding` and `Accept-Charset` are available through `req.acceptsLanguages()` etc.

### Vary
If the response changes with a header, add `res.vary('Accept')` so caches store separate versions.

### CORS headers
Cross-origin rules are also just headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`); see the CORS topic.
keyPoints: `req.get(name)` reads, `res.set(name, value)` writes headers
Cookies need `cookie-parser` to be read; set with `res.cookie`
Cookie security flags: `httpOnly`, `secure`, `sameSite`, `maxAge`
`res.format()` and `req.accepts()` implement content negotiation
Remove the `X-Powered-By` header
pitfalls: `maxAge` confusion: it is milliseconds in Express (seconds in the raw header)
Clearing a cookie with different path/domain options than it was set with

examples.title: Cookies and res.format
Negotiation in action
examples.code: curl -H "Accept: application/json" localhost:3000/report # {"total":42} curl -H "Accept: text/html" localhost:3000/report # Total: 42 curl -H "Accept: image/png" localhost:3000/report # Not Acceptable (406) curl -i localhost:3000/set-theme/dark # Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Max-Age=604800; Path=/; Expires=...; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

interview.q: What is the difference between a signed and a normal cookie?
interview.a: A signed cookie carries an HMAC made with your secret so tampering is detected, but its content is still readable; it is integrity, not secrecy.

interview.q: How do you serve JSON or HTML from the same route?
interview.a: Use res.format() (or req.accepts) to branch on the Accept header and return 406 if nothing matches.

topics.title: Streaming, Compression, ETag and Caching
topics.summary: Stream large payloads, gzip responses and use ETag/Cache-Control so clients and CDNs reuse data.
topics.description:
### Streaming
Reading a big file into memory (`fs.readFile`) before sending wastes RAM and delays the first byte. Streams send data in chunks:

```js
import { pipeline } from 'node:stream/promises'
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream('big.csv'), res)
```

`res` is a writable stream. `pipeline` handles errors and back-pressure and cleans up if the client disconnects. `res.sendFile` and `express.static` already stream.

### Compression
The `compression` middleware gzips/brotli-compresses responses larger than 1 KB when the client sends `Accept-Encoding`. Typically cuts JSON/HTML size by 70 percent or more. In production, nginx or a CDN often does this instead.

### ETag and conditional requests
Express automatically adds a weak **ETag** (hash of the body) to `res.send/json` responses. When the browser sends `If-None-Match` with the same tag, Express replies **304 Not Modified** with no body, saving bandwidth. The server still did the work, though.

### Cache-Control
Tell clients and CDNs how long they may reuse a response:
| Header | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600` | anyone may cache for 1 hour |
| `Cache-Control: private, max-age=60` | only the browser may cache |
| `Cache-Control: no-store` | never cache (sensitive data) |
| `Cache-Control: no-cache` | must revalidate every time |

For static assets use `express.static(dir, { maxAge: '1y', immutable: true })` with hashed file names (Vite does this); keep `index.html` uncached.
keyPoints: Stream files with `pipeline(stream, res)` instead of reading them fully
`compression()` middleware shrinks text responses; proxies can do it too
Express sets weak ETags, giving 304 responses for unchanged data
`Cache-Control` controls browser/CDN caching: public, private, no-store, no-cache
Long cache for hashed assets, none for HTML and private API data
pitfalls: Caching authenticated responses with `public` (data leaks between users)
Compressing already-compressed files like JPEG or ZIP (wasted CPU)
Using `readFile` for multi-GB files and exhausting memory

examples.title: Streaming, compression and cache headers
Seeing ETag and 304
examples.code:
$ curl -i localhost:3000/api/countries
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600
ETag: W/"1d-abc123..."

$ curl -i localhost:3000/api/countries -H 'If-None-Match: W/"1d-abc123..."'
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

interview.a: Not Modified: the client's cached copy (identified by ETag or Last-Modified) is still valid, so no body is sent.

interview.q: Why stream instead of reading a file fully?
interview.a: Streaming keeps memory low and starts sending immediately, because data is passed in small chunks with back-pressure handling.
